newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia's Tudjman rejects EU cooperation demands.
newsitem.headline: Croatia's Tudjman rejects EU cooperation demands.

text.p: Croatian President Franjo Tudjman on Wednesday urged minority Serbs in their last rebel enclave to participate in March elections and rejected what he said were Western demands for a political alliance of Balkan countries.

The 74-year old leader, reportedly ill with inoperable cancer, also made clear presidential elections would be held this year as scheduled but did not say whether he would run for his third term in office.

"From this place I call upon all the Serbs (in the Eastern Slavonia enclave) to take part in the voting for local adminstrative bodies," he told the parliament in his annual "state of the nation" speech.

The president looked pale and wore face powder, but his voice did not waver during the two-hour long speech which was moderate in tone and did not fulfil advance speculation that he might resign or announce dramatic constitutional changes.
Instead he said "any substantial changes to the constitution are out of the question" and called for a "unity of all Croatian political parties on the issues of national security and progress".

In the concluding remarks described as tasks for 1997, Tudjman said: "Of course, the presidential election is of no lesser importance. It is the state administration's duty to create conditions so it can be carried out normally".
The nationalist strongman rejected a European Union-backed idea of a Balkan alliance and proposed a constitutional amendment to enhance the country's independence.
"We should add a new article -- a constitutional ban on attempts to merge Croatia with any Yugoslav or Balkan state or federation," Tudjman said to loud applause.
The EU has made its acceptance of countries that emerged after the fall of communism conditional on a boost in their economic and political cooperation.
Croatia sees the move as an attempt to revive federal Yugoslavia, from which it seceded in 1991.

Croatia said earlier this month it agreed in principle with a U.S. initiative called SECI (Southeast European Cooperation Initiative), after its founder, U.S. diplomat Richard Schifter, met Tudjman in Zagreb.
SECI aims explicitly for economic cooperation, including common markets and soft borders, between 12 Balkan countries.
Tudjman criticised the SECI initiative but admitted it was "somewhat different" from the EU's regional approach.
"With the U.S. initiative Croatia would find itself even deeper in the Balkans," he said of his country, which boasts of centuries-old ties with central Europe and the Mediterranean.

"The links with the Balkans were a short episode in our history. These (EU) initiatives would bring about economic regression and destroy all we've done. Therefore we can't accept anything like that."
He added that Croatia was ready to "have good neighbourly relations and cooperate with those countries".
In his remarks to the Serbs, Tudjman said some militants were still resisting Eastern Slavonia's reintegration and were "making unrealistic demands for political autonomy".
"But we have guaranteed them all their rights," he said.

Croatia recently offered a human and minority rights package which the Serbs dismissed as unsatisfactory, demanding that the area remain a single administrative unit instead of being divided into two counties in line with the constitution.
The mandate of 5,000 U.N. peacekeepers overseeing the reintegration expires on July 15, after which Zagreb wants to take full control of the enclave.
